title: Superposition

parts.text:
28 A parallel beam of light of wavelength 600 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The
grating has 300 lines per millimetre.
What is the total number of intensity maxima from the grating?
A
1
B
3
C
11
D
13

hints: Convert the 300 lines per millimetre into the grating spacing $d$ in metres for the 600 nm light.
Use $d \sin\theta = n\lambda$ with the limiting case $\sin\theta = 1$ to find the largest possible order $n$.
Remember to count maxima on both sides of the normal plus the $n = 0$ central maximum, and round the calculated $n$ down to an integer.
walkthrough: Find the grating spacing from 300 lines per millimetre: $d = 1/300 \text{ mm} = 3.33 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}$.
State the grating equation for normal incidence: $d \sin\theta = n\lambda$ with $\lambda = 600 \text{ nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$.
The largest order occurs at the largest angle, $\theta = 90^\circ$, so $\sin\theta = 1$ and $n_{max} = d/\lambda$.
Substitute values: $n_{max} = (3.33 \times 10^{-6})/(600 \times 10^{-9}) = 5.55$, so only integer orders up to $n = 5$ are possible.
Count all maxima: $n = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1$ on each side plus $n = 0$ in the centre, giving $2 \times 5 + 1 = 11$.

A.explanation: Only 1 maximum would mean only the zero order exists, which ignores the higher orders allowed because $d$ is larger than $\lambda$.

B.explanation: 3 maxima would mean only $n = 0$ and $n = 1$ on each side, which underestimates the maximum order given by $d/\lambda$.

C.explanation: Maximum order is $n = 5$ from $d \sin 90^\circ = n\lambda$, so total maxima are $2 \times 5 + 1 = 11$.

D.explanation: 13 maxima would need $n = 6$, but $n = 6$ requires $\sin\theta > 1$ since $6 \times 600\text{ nm}$ exceeds the slit spacing.
